claims.text: The as-prepared selected high-entropy alloy has a random multi-element distribution.
The selected alloy crystallizes in a bcc structure.
The as-prepared alloy may have variable microstructural homogeneity.
Thermal annealing or related processing will increase atomic homogeneity while producing a consistently uniform bcc phase.
Superconducting transitions in the selected alloy should be detectable below approximately 10 K at ambient pressure.
High mixing entropy stabilizes a homogeneous bcc crystal structure.
A homogeneous bcc structure promotes spatially uniform electron–phonon coupling.
Uniform electron–phonon coupling enables a conventional type-II superconducting state.
High mixing entropy suppresses phase separation and local structural inhomogeneities.
Structural stability and homogeneity minimize electron scattering and spatial fluctuations in electron–phonon interactions.
Reduced scattering and electron–phonon fluctuations reinforce Cooper-pair formation.
The annealed sample will have a clearer and sharper superconducting transition than the as-prepared sample.
The annealed sample may have a higher critical temperature than the as-prepared sample.
The annealed sample will have enhanced critical fields relative to the as-prepared sample.
Greater bcc-phase uniformity will correlate with improved superconducting properties.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy retains its high-mixing-entropy-induced bcc structure.
Compositional fluctuations, secondary phases, or extreme lattice-disrupting perturbations can invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Related high-entropy-alloy superconductors exhibit robust superconductivity, including robustness under very high pressure.
Failure of annealing to produce a statistically significant improvement in Tc, transition sharpness, or Hc2 would falsify the homogeneity-enhancement hypothesis.
